definition: topic_consistency — continuity with the input: the share of the output's content-bearing sentences that connect to the input's topic must be at least a third (config key topic_consistency, default 0.33). A sentence connects when it shares a content term with the input or with an earlier connected sentence; list items are read under the sentence that introduces them; outputs with fewer than six words of four or more letters are skipped rather than judged. Definition version: docs/api-reference.md §Relevance Rules and the rule description as merged in #416 (9d9fd50) on 2026-09-04, which replaced the share-of-output-words-found-in-the-input measure. Positive = fewer than a third of the content sentences connect (the rule should FAIL).
source: LLM-authored on 2026-09-04; cases marked "real transcript t-NN" carry the real input/output pair (and token/cost figures where used) from a 2026-09-03 UAT run of an agent against the read-only Iris repository at v0.6.0.
labelling: LLM-authored on 2026-09-04 and labelled against the documented definition. First labelled that morning semantically against the definition then documented (5% of output words found in the input, purpose "stays on topic"); re-labelled the same day, after #416 replaced the mechanism with sentence continuity, by applying the new documented definition independently by script — its sentence splitting, content-term lists and inflection folding are this file's own reading, not the rule's — with each note stating the connected/total count that decided the label. Consequences a reader should know: an off-target real answer that reuses the question's vocabulary connects (t-17, t-18 are negative), and an on-topic answer in fresh words does not (three such cases are positive; the documentation states this lexical limit). 0 case(s) landed between 20% and 45% under this reading and were dropped as undecidable from the documentation alone: none. Four cases whose point was that a shared word is not topical relevance (history of the same product, business retention for a database question) were removed because the documented definition explicitly reads a shared term as connection, so they cannot be labelled positive under it. Real-transcript cases carry the real input and output.

cases.label: negative
cases.input: Summarise the install section of README.md for me — what are the ways to install Iris and what is the one-liner?
cases.output:
Iris installs as an MCP server; there is no separate install step beyond pointing your MCP client at it. From README.md ("Hook up your own agent" through "Other Install Methods"):

1. One-block MCP config (the one-liner). Add this to your client's MCP config:
```json
{ "mcpServers": { "iris-eval": { "command": "npx", "args": ["@iris-eval/mcp-server", "--dashboard"] } } }
```
The agent discovers nine tools on connect and the dashboard serves at http://localhost:6920. Drop --dashboard from the args to run headless; you can open the dashboard any time with `npx @iris-eval/mcp-server --dashboard`.

2. Per-client recipes for the same block: Claude Desktop (edit claude_desktop_config.json, restart), Claude Code (`claude mcp add --transport stdio iris-eval -- npx @iris-eval/mcp-server`, then restart the session; on Windows do not wrap it in cmd /c), Cursor/Windsurf (.cursor/mcp.json), VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json, which uses "servers" not "mcpServers"), Cline (MCP Servers panel), Zed (context_servers in settings.json), OpenAI Codex CLI (~/.codex/config.toml), Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json). Anything else that speaks MCP works with the same npx command.

3. Global install: `npm install -g @iris-eval/mcp-server` then `iris-mcp --dashboard`. Recommended for persistent data and faster startup; traces live at ~/.iris/iris.db either way, npx is just slower to start.

4. Docker: `docker run -p 3000:3000 -p 6920:6920 -v iris-data:/data ghcr.io/iris-eval/mcp-server`. Port 3000 is the MCP HTTP transport, 6920 is the dashboard, which also serves the POST /api/v1/traces ingest endpoint.

Verify with `npx @iris-eval/mcp-server --self-test` (exit 0 = healthy, runs in an isolated temp home) and `--version`. Everything Iris writes lives under ~/.iris, or wherever IRIS_HOME points.

Two caveats the section calls out: MCP tools only fire when the model decides to call them, so use POST /api/v1/traces when capture must not depend on the model; and that endpoint exists only while the dashboard is running, and accepts unauthenticated writes unless you start Iris with --api-key.
cases.notes: real transcript t-01: summarises the install section as asked; nearly every sentence connects (16/17 content sentences connect = 94% by this file's reading of the definition)

cases.input: What does the --purge flag do? Read src/index.ts, not the docs.
cases.output:
--purge is a one-shot maintenance mode, not a server option. From src/index.ts:

- What it does (help text, line 145): deletes EVERY stored trace, span and evaluation from the configured database, compacts the file and truncates the write-ahead log so the deleted text does not linger on disk, then exits. Deployed rules, the audit log and preferences are kept. Not reversible. Stop any running Iris server first, because the file is compacted in place.
- How (runPurge, line 269): opens the configured storage, calls storage.purge(LOCAL_TENANT), prints "iris-mcp: purged N trace(s) and M evaluation(s) from <path> (database compacted, write-ahead log truncated). Deployed rules, audit log and preferences were kept." to stderr, closes storage and exits 0. Any error prints "purge failed: …" and exits 1.
- Constraints: it is one of four mutually exclusive mode flags (demo, demo-clear, self-test, purge), so combining it with another mode is refused, and --purge --dashboard is refused with an explicit message because purge exits as soon as it finishes and nothing would be served. It runs against the configured database, never the demo one (--demo-clear handles that).
- Why it exists (comment for #372): the retention sweep only ever trimmed by age, and deleting iris.db by hand left every row readable in iris.db-wal. This is the one-command answer to "remove everything Iris stored about my agents".
cases.notes: real transcript t-03: explains --purge from src/index.ts as asked (12/13 content sentences connect = 92% by this file's reading of the definition)

cases.input: What does eval_type: "all" return? Answer from the engine source, not the docs.
cases.output:
eval_type "all" is handled by EvalEngine.evaluateAll() in src/eval/engine.ts, not by the single-bundle evaluate().

What runs: for every type in ALL_EVAL_TYPES (completeness, relevance, safety, cost, custom) it collects the built-in bundle plus any rules deployed under that type, tags each with its category, then appends the call's inline custom_rules tagged "custom". Everything runs in ONE pass through this.run("all", rules, categories, context), sharing a single regex budget, so the whole call is bounded exactly like a single bundle.

What comes back: an ordinary EvalResult whose eval_type is "all" — id, score, passed, rule_results, suggestions, rules_evaluated, rules_skipped, insufficient_data. The overall verdict is the same arithmetic as a single bundle applied to every rule that ran: weighted score against the threshold, with the critical veto spanning all bundles (a no_pii failure fails the whole thing). Because categories were passed, the result also carries a categories map (Partial<Record<EvalType, EvalCategoryResult>>) with the same arithmetic computed per bundle, and each rule_result carries a category so a reader can regroup them. Rules that lack their context (expected for expected_coverage, input for the two relevance rules, cost or token usage for the cost rules) report as skipped rather than failing.
cases.notes: real transcript t-05: explains eval_type "all" from the engine source: every sentence connects through the chain even though the vocabulary is the engine's (7/7 content sentences connect = 100% by this file's reading of the definition)

cases.input: Describe the jobs in .github/workflows/release.yml and how they depend on each other.
cases.output:
release.yml runs on a pushed v* tag, or by manual workflow_dispatch against an existing tag to re-run a failed release. Six jobs; the header comment states the graph and the needs: lines confirm it.

1. validate — checks the tag matches package.json, that every version-carrying file agrees, and that CHANGELOG.md has a section for the version.
2. publish-npm (needs validate) — verifies package integrity, generates an npm SBOM, determines the dist-tag (a tag containing "-" is a prerelease), publishes with npm Trusted Publishing over OIDC so there is no NPM_TOKEN secret, then attests and uploads the SBOM.
3. publish-docker (needs validate) — determines image tags, builds and pushes a multi-arch image to GHCR, signs it by digest with cosign (keyless, same OIDC identity), and generates, attests and uploads a Docker SBOM.
4. github-release (needs publish-npm and publish-docker) — signs the SBOMs with cosign, determines the release type, composes the release body from CHANGELOG.md and creates the GitHub release.
5. publish-registry (needs publish-npm; production tags only, skipped when the tag contains "-") — installs a pinned mcp-publisher, validates server.json, waits for npm to serve the version, checks whether it is already on the MCP Registry, authenticates with GitHub OIDC, publishes, and verifies the registry's latest is this version.
6. verify-release (needs all four of publish-npm, publish-docker, github-release, publish-registry; runs when the first three succeeded and publish-registry succeeded or was skipped) — reads back from the outside: the npm dist-tag resolves to this version, the GHCR version tag and :latest resolve to the pushed digest, the GitHub release is published with SBOMs and notes attached, and on production tags the MCP Registry latest is this version. The header is explicit that this is the only job whose green means the release happened.

Permissions are contents:read at the top level; each publishing job declares its own writes (id-token: write for the OIDC token) at job level.
cases.notes: real transcript t-06: describes the release workflow jobs; every sentence connects (10/10 content sentences connect = 100% by this file's reading of the definition)

cases.input: Give me a one-paragraph description of Iris for our internal wiki.
cases.output:
Iris is an open-source (MIT) MCP server that scores every agent run for quality, safety and cost on your own machine, with no SDK and no account. Runs land in a local SQLite database, where 13 deterministic built-in rules check for PII and credential leaks, prompt injection, hallucination markers, stub output and cost thresholds without any LLM calls; an optional bring-your-own-key LLM judge with a hard per-eval cost cap handles the semantic questions, and a citation verifier checks that cited sources actually support their claims. It exposes nine MCP tools and a dashboard on port 6920, ingests traces over plain HTTP for capture that does not depend on the model choosing to log, and never sends traces anywhere (no telemetry). Every rule is inspectable and editable. Requires Node.js 20 or later.

cases.input: What does the no_stub_output rule check for?
cases.output: no_stub_output is a completeness check with three parts: the output must meet a minimum character length (default 50, configurable through min_output_length or min_length, with partial credit of length/min below it), must not be empty or whitespace-only (weight 2, a hard 0 if it is), and must contain at least 2 sentences (split on . ! ?, weight 0.5). There is also an expected_coverage component that only runs when an expected text is supplied and passes when at least 50% of the expected terms appear in the output. If those pass, the output is not considered a stub.

cases.input: How many built-in rules does Iris ship and what are they? Start from src/eval/rules/index.ts.
cases.output:
13 built-in rules. src/eval/rules/index.ts maps each eval type to a bundle (custom is an empty bundle by design, it only ever holds deployed rules), and the four bundles export:

- completeness (4): min_output_length, non_empty_output, sentence_count, expected_coverage
- relevance (2): keyword_overlap, topic_consistency
- safety (5): no_pii, no_blocklist_words, no_injection_patterns, no_stub_output, no_hallucination_markers
- cost (2): cost_under_threshold, token_efficiency

4 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 13. Three of the safety rules (no_pii, no_blocklist_words, no_injection_patterns) are marked critical, so a failure on any of them forces the overall evaluation to passed=false regardless of the weighted score; no_stub_output and no_hallucination_markers deliberately are not.
